<reason>PRO built a clean functional case (same business, same risks, same rules) and its strongest weighing point—protections in force beat protections in a draft—was real and forced CON to admit no comprehensive federal crypto statute binds platforms today. But CON consistently converted PRO's own moves into damage: the wheat/commodity-broker analogy conceded that a non-securities regime can deliver segregation and capital with teeth; PRO's honest "almost none" on tZERO/Prometheum volume became "a locked cabinet with excellent tools"; and PRO's "none directly" on FTX reach conceded the offshore point. CON then narrowed the motion to "which box," argued the exchange box cannot legally list Bitcoin/Ether/stablecoins (most of the market), and when PRO retreated to the broker-dealer prong, CON's claim that customer-property rules cover securities and cash rather than Bitcoin balances was met only with "the examiner sees the same page"—which CON dispatched with "seeing is not segregating." PRO could have pressed harder that the motion's alternative as written is a *lightly* supervised category and CON's Japan/EU model is not that, but PRO only gestured at this. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 and the late New York state-regime mention are small execution costs, not enough to offset its sharper, more adaptive rebuttals. Both sides were well grounded; neither used fake precision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 turning PRO's wheat example: commodity brokers are supervised under commodity law, not as securities broker-dealers, so PRO had conceded a non-securities regime can carry segregation and capital rules—collapsing PRO's "they conceded my case" framing and reframing the debate onto which statutory box, where CON's listing-prohibition and custody-rule-scope points then went largely unrebutted.</best_rebuttal>
